EICMA 2026 • Here Are Some of the Serious and Obscure Brands That EICMA 2026 Had To Offer – Worth Knowing About
Winningest Hemi Cuda Ever: Totaled in 1970, Won 45 Races in Five Years, You Never Heard of It
85 photos
Photo: Bring A Trailer/1600veloce
What's the winningest Hemi Cuda ever? While American drag strips usually claim the most famous Plymouth muscle cars, the undisputed global champion actually conquered the most un-American race tracks ever. Literally, and figuratively. This 1970 Plymouth ‘Cuda 4-speed and its 426 Hemi triumphed in road racing in France in a way no other Mopar did. And it’s for sale.
We’re having a downpour of blue 1970 racing royalty over at Bring a Trailer, apparently. A few days ago, Carl Tasca’s 1970 Boss 429 drag car was listed, sporting Richard Petty’s Boss 429 V8. And now, it’s Henri Chemin’s former champion E-body’s turn to heat up the bidding wars, after its glorious triumphs on the winding circuits and mountain climbs of Europe, more than 50 years ago.
Meet chassis BS23R0B249759, the factory-backed 1970 Plymouth Hemi 'Cuda 4-speed campaigned by Ecurie Chrysler, Ma’ Mopar’s French division. Between 1970 and 1974, this extraordinary machine captured 45 documented Group 1 victories across fierce European road races and grueling French Alpine hillclimbs.
Understanding how a heavy Detroit bruiser dominated European motorsport requires a bit motoring archivistic shoveling. Launched in 1964 on the compact A-body platform shared with the economical Valiant, the early Barracuda featured a distinctive wraparound glass fastback and an optional 273-cubic-inch V8.
Photo: Bring A Trailer/1600veloce A redesigned second generation arrived in 1967 with dedicated sheet metal, offering notchback, fastback, and convertible bodies paired with optional 340-cubic-inch, 383-cubic-inch, and 440-cubic-inch performance engines.
The legend of the Hemi Barracuda began in 1968 when Chrysler stuffed its 426-cubic-inch Hemi V8 into 50 lightweight A-body fastbacks strictly for Super Stock drag racing. Everything changed for the 1970 model year when Plymouth abandoned the A-body architecture for the wider, lower E-body platform shared with the Dodge Challenger. The bigger body came about precisely to give the big-blocks proper accommodation.
The performance-oriented 'Cuda trim finally brought the 425-horsepower 7.0-liter Hemi V8 to regular public showroom floors across America. Equipped with a functional Shaker hood scoop, heavy-duty suspension, and dual 4-barrel Carter AFB carburetors, the E-body Hemi 'Cuda became the ultimate symbol of raw American muscle.
Photo: Bring A Trailer/1600veloce High insurance premiums and steep sticker prices kept production numbers remarkably low overall. Plymouth built just 652 Hemi 'Cuda hardtops and 14 convertibles for 1970, followed by 108 hardtops and 7 convertibles in 1971 before tightening emissions regulations put down the legendary engine.
In North American motorsport, E-body Mopars waged war on two major fronts during 1970. When the National Hot Rod Association introduced its heads-up Pro Stock category for the 1970 season, legendary drag racing duo Ronnie Sox and Buddy Martin campaigned a 4-speed Hemi 'Cuda that dominated quarter-mile drag strips across 1970 and 1971.
Simultaneously, Chrysler targeted road racing by officially entering the prestigious Sports Car Club of America Trans-Am Championship. Chrysler commissioned Dan Gurney and his All American Racers team to build three factory Plymouth Barracudas for the 1970 Trans-Am season alongside the sister Dodge Challenge r T/A program.
Photo: Bring A Trailer/1600veloce Driven by Gurney and young teammate Swede Savage, those acid-dipped racers used destroked 303.8-cubic-inch V8 engines producing 450 horsepower, titanium suspension upright components, and computer-designed roll cages, while spawning 2,724 street-legal AAR 'Cuda homologation models powered by 340-cubic-inch Six Pack V8 engines.
While American teams battled unsuccessfully in Trans-Am, an even more remarkable E-body racing story unfolded across the Atlantic Ocean in France. Having steadily acquired shares in French automaker Simca since 1958, Chrysler formalized its Chrysler France subsidiary in 1970, which also encompassed Matra Automobiles.
Competition director Henri Chemin, who previously led Ford France's racing and public relations programs, launched Ecurie Chrysler France and ordered four Plymouth 'Cudas for spirited European competition.
Photo: Bring A Trailer/1600veloce The centerpiece of that French fleet was chassis BS23R0B249759, a 1970 Hemi 'Cuda built to export specifications in Alpine White over black vinyl bucket seats with the A33 Track Pak, an A833 4-speed manual transmission, and a 3.54:1 axle. Registered under French license plate 6752 WK 75, the coupe received crucial chassis tuning from Matra race engineers, who realigned the front brake calipers, adjusted ballast, and relocated dual batteries in the trunk.
Deciphering the original fender tag reveals how Hamtramck assembly line 1 configured this Plymouth 'Cuda 2-door hardtop. Finished in Alpine White paint over high-grade black vinyl trim with full door panels, it paired the 426-cubic-inch Hemi V8 and 4-speed manual transmission with the A33 Track Pak and 26-inch radiator.
Interior appointments included bucket seats, a woodgrain console, power windows, and a Rallye cluster with a tachometer and a 150-mph speedo (quite strange, for an export to Europe car). Additional factory equipment comprised power brakes, a Shaker sport hood with tie-down pins, fender turn signals, a right-hand racing mirror, dual exhaust with chrome tips, and drip rail, wide sill, and rear deck moldings throughout the exterior body.
Photo: Bring A Trailer/1600veloce Most intriguing is the rare N31 code, listed on the broadcast sheet under “N” engine accessories as optional compression ratio. Instead of a bespoke ratio, N31 always lowered compression to roughly 8.0:1 to 8.5:1 for domestic government or fleet vehicles avoiding costly premium fuel. On this export Hemi 'Cuda, it accommodated lower-octane European gasoline through reduced compression, re-jetted carburetors, and a specifically recurved ignition distributor.
Chemin immediately excelled in 1970, winning nine events at venues including Autun and Turckheim to secure Ecurie Chrysler France's first circuit championship. Disaster struck on August 23, 1970, at the Brides-Méribel hillclimb when power steering failure sent Chemin plunging 65 feet into a steep wooded ravine.
With the shell ruined, mechanics transferred the original engine, transmission, driveline, dashboard, and gauges into a replacement body (promptly sourced from a 440-Six-Barrel car bought alongside the Hemi car), returning to competition the following month. I don’t know the undersides and nuances of French automobile governing bodies, but the rebodied pony car kept the VIN from the original shell, although that had been deemed a total loss.
Photo: Bring A Trailer/1600veloce Rebuilt and unstoppable, the Plymouth achieved its peak in 1971, earning 16 victories at circuits including Albi, Montlhéry, Magny-Cours, and Paul Ricard. When the original 426-cubic-inch Hemi failed mid-season, mechanics installed the engine from a 1971 team car, chassis BS23R1B215686. Chemin added 7 wins in 1972 for circuit and hillclimb titles, before Jean-François Mas scored 12 victories in 1973 and privateer Jean-Claude Géral won a hillclimb at Charnizay in 1974.
After retiring from competition, the Equipe Alméras Frères team sold the ' Cuda in 1976 to a Lyon buyer who painted it white and kept it until 2007. The caretaker who got it stored the racer in a barn for five years until the current owner bought it in 2012. Imported to America, the coupe underwent a comprehensive restoration by Redline Restorations in Bridgeport, Connecticut, conducted in direct consultation with Henri Chemin.
Photo: Bring A Trailer/1600veloce Refinished in its 1971 French-Blue-and-white livery with Shell and Cibie graphics, the coupe features 15-inch steel wheels, an 8.75-inch axle, a Hurst pistol-grip shifter, a 150-mph speedometer, and an 8,000-rpm tachometer. In 2013, the owner recovered the original matching-numbers 0B249759 engine block after decades in France and Canada. Honored at Greenwich and Hershey, the restored Plymouth returned to France in 2014 so Chemin could lap historic Circuit Paul Ricard again.
Now, this historic 1970 Plymouth Hemi 'Cuda is offered for sale at no reserve on Bring a Trailer by New York dealer 1600Veloce, complete with its spare original engine block, period scrapbooks, FIVA identity card, and upcoming display at Retromobile New York. As collectors pursue this 45-time race winner, the current bid stands at $110,000 with 10 days left on the auction clock. Is it going to go into seven figures?
Via // Bring A Trailer
